correctness.rationale: The one-to-one scalar-normalized correspondence to projective coincidence points is checked. A nonzero binary cubic bounds N by three. Sharp 1-,2-,3-transitivity counts the ordered fixed-point incidences, with weights explicitly determined by squaring fibers. Triangular moment inversion gives the complete odd and even laws, including all boundary fields. A separate exhaustive finite-field direct checker covers nine field orders and confirms both counts and moments; no computation is substituted for an all-q proof.

Geometric multiplicity-stratum counts do not specify how distinct roots split over Fq. The earlier even-field law does not imply the odd-field branch: projective squaring ceases to be bijective when q is odd. The survey predicts only an asymptotic S3 law via Chebotarev, not the exact corrections or universal zero proportion.

originality.rationale: The new content is an exact finite-q rational-idempotent distribution in dimension two for all odd prime powers, including an exact zero probability of 1/3; the principal 2026 source states mean and asymptotic law, not this law. The proof supplies the missing third factorial moment via projective three-point incidence. Geometric-root multiplicities, prior second moments, and isomorphism-class counts do not determine the asserted rational splitting probabilities. Historical risk from a broader random-projectivity or binary-cubic theorem remains.
residual_risks: A stronger historical result on random projectivities, binary cubic factorization, or finite-field quadratic rational maps may imply this specialization without matching the vocabulary of evolution algebras.

value.rationale: This is the complete exact finite-q rational-idempotent probability law for the minimal nontrivial random perfect evolution-algebra family, sharpening the 2026 source from a mean and asymptotic S3 prediction to exact probabilities. The characteristic-independent 1/3 absence probability contrasts with a characteristic-dependent probability of exactly two rational idempotents and remains true over all prime-power extensions. The law has direct relevance to small-dimensional finite-field evolution-algebra statistics and is not an arbitrary parameter slice.
